A1-A2.headline: Antarctic Ice Grows in 2026

pages.text: The Antarctic is a big continent. It has an ocean all around it. Sea ice grows there in the winter. It gets bigger when it is cold. It gets smaller in the summer.

pages.text: The ice usually grows the most in September. NASA says the ice reached its top size on September 14, 2026. The ice covered 17.59 million square kilometers. This is 6.79 million square miles.

This was the third-lowest amount ever recorded. Scientists use satellites to see the ice. The satellites take pictures from space. They can see the ice even when it is cloudy. This helps them track the ice every year.
The amount of ice changes a lot. It grew from 1979 to 2014. Then it started to get smaller in 2016. The ice is often lower than normal now. Scientists want to know if this is a long-term change.

evidence: Unlike the Arctic—an ocean basin surrounded by land—the Antarctic is a large continent surrounded by an ocean.
According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Antarctic sea ice in 2026 likely reached its annual maximum extent on September 14 (above).
On that date, the ice covered an estimated 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles), making it the third-lowest maximum on record.

B1-B2.headline: Antarctic Sea Ice Reaches 2026 Maximum

pages.text: Unlike the Arctic, which is an ocean basin surrounded by land, the Antarctic is a large continent encircled by water. This geography allows sea ice to expand significantly during the winter months. However, the ice also reaches warmer latitudes, which causes more melting during the summer. Typically, Antarctic sea ice peaks in September and reaches its minimum in February.

pages.text: According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center, the ice reached its annual maximum on September 14, 2026. It covered 17.59 million square kilometers, or 6.79 million square miles. This measurement represents the third-lowest maximum ever recorded by scientists. Researchers use satellites with passive microwave sensors to monitor the ice.

These sensors detect energy emitted by the ice, allowing observations to continue regardless of cloud cover. Scientists define the total area with at least 15 percent ice concentration as the sea ice extent. Historical data shows that Antarctic sea ice increased by about 1 percent per decade between 1979 and 2014.

However, this trend shifted in 2015, and significant decreases began in 2016. Although there have been minor rebounds, overall coverage has remained lower than normal. Both the record low minimum and maximum occurred in 2023. Experts continue to study whether this decline represents a long-term change or a statistical fluctuation.

evidence: Antarctic sea ice usually peaks in September, around the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, and retreats to a minimum in February.
The images include only areas where ice concentration was at least 15 percent, a threshold scientists commonly use to count an area as ice-covered in satellite data.
Scientists will continue to observe the area each year to find out if the decline is part of a long-term change or a statistical fluctuation.

C1-C2.headline: Antarctic Sea Ice Extent Peaks in 2026

pages.text: The Antarctic, a vast continent circumscribed by the Southern Ocean, presents a distinct geographical profile compared to the Arctic basin. This configuration facilitates extensive sea ice expansion during the austral winter, yet simultaneously exposes the ice to warmer latitudes, thereby accelerating summer ablation. Historically, the ice reaches its annual zenith in September before retreating to a nadir in February.

pages.text: Data from NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center indicate that the 2026 maximum occurred on September 14. The ice extent was measured at 17.59 million square kilometers, equivalent to 6.79 million square miles, marking the third-lowest maximum in the satellite record. This assessment relies on passive microwave sensors, which penetrate cloud cover to provide consistent monitoring of ice concentration, defined by a 15 percent threshold.

The trajectory of Antarctic sea ice has been characterized by notable variability. From 1979 to 2014, the region experienced a modest increase of approximately 1 percent per decade. This period included consecutive record highs between 2012 and 2014, which contrasted sharply with the concurrent decline of Arctic ice. However, this growth trend terminated in 2015, followed by substantial decreases starting in 2016. While minor rebounds have occurred, the overall coverage has largely remained suppressed.

The year 2023 was particularly significant, witnessing both the record low minimum and maximum extents. Given the inherent volatility of these measurements, researchers remain cautious, continuing to analyze whether the current downward trend signifies a permanent long-term shift or merely a transient statistical fluctuation. This ongoing surveillance is critical for understanding the complex dynamics of Earth's surface changes as tracked through the World of Change series.

evidence: Because of this geography, sea ice has more room to expand during the winter.
However, that ice also stretches into warmer latitudes, leading to more melting in the summer.
The climb came to an end in 2015, and significant decreases in sea ice around Antarctica started to occur in 2016.
